post.description:
Replace a user's roles with the given list.

Bounded two ways for everyone but a superuser. The target must be in the caller's scope - their own institute, or their whole school for a school administrator - and is reported as not found otherwise, the same answer a missing id gets. And only the roles the caller's own role hands out (`DELEGATION` in `api/rbac/roles.py`) may be added or removed: any other role the account holds must be sent back unchanged, or the request is refused naming it. So an institute administrator can make one of their people a collection-desk admin, and cannot make anyone a school administrator - or strip that from one.

post.description: Multipart: `file` (.xlsx or .csv with `email` and optional `student_school_id` columns - download the template from `admin/student-bulk-invitations/template/`), `dry_run` and `skip_invalid` as `true`/`false`. Every row is validated: email format and uniqueness, student ID belongs to the caller's institute and has no account yet, no duplicates within the file. A dry run answers 200 with the rows and sends nothing; a real run answers 201 with the rows and `queued`, or 400 with the rows when some are invalid and `skip_invalid` is off.

get.description:
One row per recorded change, newest first, with the acting user's username and full name resolved from the users table (`actor_username` / `actor_full_name`, null for system entries or deleted users).

All filters combine with AND; the multi-value ones (`system`, `action`, `actor_type`, `entity_type`) OR their own values together, so `?action=create,delete&system=collection` reads as *(create OR delete) AND collection*. Responses are cached per query-string until the next audit write.

For aggregate views of the same data (counts by action/system/actor, daily activity, PDF/Excel exports) use `/audit-logs/report/` and its `/pdf/` and `/excel/` variants, which take exactly the same filter parameters.

post.description:
Exchanges a Google ID token for this API's access/refresh pair.

Sign-in only — it never creates an account. Refusals carry a `code` so the client can respond usefully:

- `no_account` — verified, but no account holds that address. The response echoes the `email` so the UI can name it.
- `account_inactive` — the account was deactivated.
- `email_not_verified` — invited but never activated.
- `token_expired` / `invalid_token` — retry is worth it for the first, not the second.
- `google_not_configured` / `google_unreachable` — our fault, 503.

400.description: Unusable token, or no account for that address

post.description: Creates a user using a Google ID token.

post.description:
POST `{new_email}`: an administrator starts an email change for an account in their scope. A one-time confirmation link is mailed to the NEW address and nothing to the old one - this is for the person whose old mailbox is lost, for whom the self-service flow (a code to the current address first) can never complete. The account's email does not change until that link is opened; until then the detail endpoint reports it under `pending_email_change`. Posting again, with the same or another address, replaces the pending change with a fresh link - that is how a resend works.

DELETE: cancel whatever change is pending; the emailed link stops working.

Same scope and rank rules as `set-password`: only accounts in the caller's institute (or school, for a school administrator), never the caller's own, never a superuser's, and a school administrator's only by another school administrator.
post.summary: Point an account at a new email address, or cancel a pending change

post.description:
An administrator resets the password of an account in their scope - the person has forgotten theirs and cannot use `change-password`, which needs the current one.

Scope is the same as the list: a superuser reaches any account, institute staff only the accounts of their own institute (anything else is a 404, not a 403, so the route does not confirm that an account exists outside the caller's institute). On top of that a caller may not reset their own password here, a superuser's, or that of anyone in a more senior role than their own.

Every refresh token the account holds is blacklisted, so a session that was open somewhere else is ended too - if the reason for the reset was a compromised account, a reset that left the old session signed in would not have helped.

AdminEmailChange.description:
An administrator pointing somebody ELSE's account at a new address.

`POST /users/{id}/change-email/`. The target comes through the context so
"already the email on this account" is judged against theirs. The
uniqueness rule is the platform's usual one and is re-checked when the
link is opened - the address could be claimed in between.

AdminSetPassword.description:
An administrator setting somebody ELSE's password.

`POST /users/{id}/set-password/`. Distinct from `ChangePasswordSerializer`
on purpose: that one proves you know the current password, which is the
whole point of it, and this one exists precisely because the owner does
not - a student or an officer who has forgotten theirs and asked the
institute administrator to reset it.

The target comes in through the context, not the request body, so the
password validators run against the account being changed (a password
that contains the *target's* username is the one to refuse, not one
containing the administrator's).

UserInvite.description:
One invitation, placed somewhere in the org chart.

## Who may invite whom

`group_id` is checked against `delegable_roles(request.user)` - the
`DELEGATION` table in `api/rbac/roles.py`. Before that check the
queryset was every group in the database, so anyone holding
`users.invite_user` (an institute-level grant) could post
`group_id=<School Admins>` and mint an account two levels above their
own. The console had the same table on its side and could only hide the
option; this is what closes it. The refusal names what the caller MAY
invite, because DRF's own "invalid pk" would send them looking for a
seeding problem that does not exist.

## Where the account lands

The token records the school and institute the account will belong to,
and `RegisterSerializer` copies them onto the account at activation:

    School Admins    `school_id` names the school. Superusers only - a
                     school administrator never appoints a peer. The
                     account is school-wide and has no institute; the
                     school is what `api/rbac/scoping.py` reads.
    anything else    `institute_id` names the institute. A school
                     administrator picks one in their own school; an
                     institute administrator's own institute is used,
                     and naming a different one is refused rather than
                     silently replaced.

UserRead.description:
Detailed schema for retrieving ONE account (`GET /users/{id}/`).

This is the only user serializer that renders roles. It used to send
`group_id` / `group_name` taken from `obj.groups.first()`, which was a
quiet lie: an account genuinely can hold several groups (a school
administrator who also signs clearances), and "first" is decided by row
id, so the role it reported changed depending on the order the groups
were seeded in. The console then showed one role and the assign-roles
dialog risked stripping the ones it could not see.

`groups` is the whole set. The list endpoint deliberately does NOT carry
it - see `UserReadSlimSerializer`.

Row schema for the list (`GET /users/`).

No roles here - only how many there are. Rendering the group names on

anyway, so the column was both expensive and misleading. The count is
